title: Design an Authentication System
tagline: Sign people in safely, keep them signed in, and let every service trust who they are.

statement.prompt: Design an **authentication system** for a large web and mobile product: sign up, log in, stay logged in, reset a password and let other services verify the caller.
context: You are in a 45-minute interview. Security details matter as much as boxes and arrows.
The system serves a consumer product with tens of millions of users.
Other internal services must trust identities without calling you every time.
given: About **10 million** users, logging in about **twice a day**.
80% of logins happen in a **2-hour** morning window.
Password verification takes about **100 ms** of CPU by design.
Mobile and web clients both use it.

expectations.title: Drive the conversation
expectations.body: Ask questions before drawing anything. State your assumptions out loud so they can be corrected early.

expectations.title: Use numbers
expectations.body: Turn the givens into requests per second, storage and bandwidth. Every later choice should point back to one of them.

expectations.title: Start simple, then evolve
expectations.body: Get a working version on the board first. Add caches, sharding and queues only when a number or a requirement asks for them.

expectations.title: Go deep on the hard parts
expectations.body: For this problem the hard parts are safe password storage, session and token design, and defending against common attacks without hurting availability.

expectations.title: Name the trade-offs
expectations.body: Say what you chose, what you gave up, and what would make you change your mind.

expectations.title: Think about failure
expectations.body: Point out single points of failure and say what happens when a node, a cache or a whole zone goes down.

scope_in: MFA and social login at a high level
great: Stores passwords with a **slow salted hash** and says why.
Uses **short access tokens plus revocable refresh tokens**.

concepts.def: Random data added to a password before hashing, so equal passwords hash differently.
A signed token that carries claims such as user id and expiry; anyone with the public key can verify it.
A long-lived credential used only to get new access tokens; stored server-side so it can be revoked.
Requiring a second proof, such as a code from an app, in addition to a password.
An extension to the OAuth code flow that stops a stolen authorization code from being used.
Trying username/password pairs leaked elsewhere, hoping people reused them.

numbers: 10M users x 2 logins = 20M/day; peak window gives about **2,200 logins/s**
Password hash target about **100 ms**, so peak needs hundreds of cores
Access tokens: **about 15 minutes**; refresh tokens: days to weeks, rotated

takeaways: Store only **Argon2/bcrypt salted hashes**; never log or email passwords.
Use a **15-minute access token + rotating, revocable refresh token**.
Verify tokens **at the gateway without calling auth**; an auth outage then only affects new logins.
Defend with **rate limits, MFA, HttpOnly cookies and identical error messages**.

steps.title: What must the system do?
steps.prompt: Pick the **core** features of an authentication system.
steps.hint: Which part says who you are, not what you can do?
steps.explain: Authentication answers **who are you?** Authorization answers **what may you do?** Keep them apart in the interview.

notes: Core: sign up, log in/out, reset password, MFA, token verification for other services

options.text: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
options.why: Passwords alone are not enough for serious products.

options.text: Password reset by email
options.why: People forget passwords constantly.

options.text: Sign up and log in with email and password
options.why: The basic flow.

options.text: Let other services verify who the caller is
options.why: Authentication is useless if nothing trusts it.

options.text: Define what each user is allowed to do on every resource (full authorization)
options.why: Related but separate. Mention it, then park it.

options.text: Keep the user logged in and log out
options.why: Sessions or tokens.

steps.title: Qualities
steps.hint: What is the cost of a mistake?
steps.explain: **Security > availability > latency.** Note the asymmetry: login is *rare and heavy*, token verification is *constant and light*.

notes: Qualities: security first, highly available, fast token verification, handles login spikes

options.text: High availability: if login is down, the whole product is down
options.why: Every user action depends on it.

options.text: Low latency on token checks (the hot path)
options.why: Every API call pays for it.

options.text: Eventual consistency of passwords across regions after a change
options.why: A changed or stolen password must take effect immediately.

options.text: Security first: protect credentials and sessions
options.why: One breach is catastrophic.

options.text: Scales for login spikes (9 am)
options.why: Bursty traffic.

steps.title: Login load
steps.prompt: **10 million** users log in on average **twice a day**, mostly in a **2-hour** morning window (80% of logins). What is the peak **logins per second**?
steps.hint: Concentrate 80% of the day's logins into the busy window.
steps.explain: About **2,200 logins per second at peak**. At 100 ms of CPU each that is **220 CPU cores busy** just hashing. This is why login capacity is planned separately from token checks, which are tens of thousands per second but nearly free.

notes: Load: ~2,200 logins/s at peak; ~100 ms CPU per password check

work: 80% in 2 hours = 16,000,000 / 7,200 s = about **2,200 per second**
Password hashing is deliberately slow (about 100 ms CPU each)

steps.title: Storing passwords
steps.hint: Make an attacker's job slow even with your database.
steps.explain: **Never store or log passwords.** Store `argon2(salt, password)` and the parameters. Re-hash when you raise the cost.

notes: Passwords: Argon2/bcrypt with unique salt per user; never log or store plain text

steps.pitfall: Fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256 for passwords.
steps.followup: Why does a unique salt matter if the hash is already slow?

options.text: A fast hash such as SHA-256 without a salt
options.why: Fast to brute-force, identical passwords look identical.

options.text: Only a **slow, salted hash** (Argon2, bcrypt or scrypt) with a unique salt per user
options.why: Slow makes guessing expensive; salts defeat precomputed tables.

options.text: Plain text in an encrypted disk
options.why: Disk encryption does not protect against an application-level breach.

options.text: Encrypted with a key so support can read them back
options.why: Anyone with the key (or a breach) gets every password.

steps.title: Sessions or tokens?
steps.prompt: Pick a way to stay logged in that scales across many services and still allows logging out.
steps.hint: What is cheap to check and what is easy to revoke?
steps.explain: **Access token = fast but short; refresh token = slow path but revocable.** Rotate refresh tokens and treat reuse as a theft signal.

notes: Tokens: 15-min signed access token + revocable rotating refresh token

steps.followup: A refresh token is stolen. How do you notice and respond?

options.text: Store the password in a cookie and re-check each time
options.why: Terrible.

options.text: A single JWT valid for 30 days
options.why: Cannot be revoked if stolen.

options.text: A session id checked in the database on every request
options.why: Works, but makes the database a bottleneck for every API call.

options.text: A short-lived signed access token (about 15 min) plus a long-lived refresh token stored (hashed) server-side and revocable
options.why: Fast stateless checks plus a way to revoke.

steps.title: The login flow
steps.prompt: Order the steps of a secure login with MFA.
steps.hint: Stop abuse early, spend CPU later.
steps.explain: Order matters: **limit, verify, challenge, issue, record.** Also give the same error for unknown users and wrong passwords.

notes: Login: HTTPS -> rate limit -> verify hash -> MFA -> issue tokens + audit log

items.text: The client sends credentials over HTTPS to the auth service
The rate limiter checks attempts for this account and IP
items.why: Cheapest check first; stops brute force.

items.text: The service looks up the user and verifies the salted hash
MFA: the user enters a one-time code
items.why: Second factor after the password passes.

items.text: Tokens are issued, the session is recorded, an audit event is written
items.why: Everything needed to review or revoke later.

steps.title: Checking tokens on every request
steps.prompt: Thousands of API calls arrive per second. Where and how are tokens verified?
steps.hint: Can verification avoid a network round trip?
steps.explain: **Stateless verification** is why JWT-style tokens scale. Keep a small, cached **revocation list** for emergency cases.

notes: Verification: gateway checks token signature/expiry locally; small cached revocation list

options.text: Each request calls the auth service to validate
options.why: Auth becomes the bottleneck and a single point of failure.

options.text: Verify only on login
options.why: Stolen or expired tokens would work forever.

options.text: At the API gateway, verifying the signature and expiry locally with a public key
options.why: No network call; services can trust the gateway's verdict.

options.text: Do not verify, trust the user id sent by the client
options.why: Anyone could claim to be anyone.

steps.title: Attacks to defend against
steps.explain: Name threats **with their defence**. A list of attacks with no fixes sounds like you only read the headlines.

notes: Threats handled: credential stuffing, XSS (HttpOnly cookies), enumeration, phishing (MFA/passkeys)

options.text: Credential stuffing (leaked passwords reused): rate limits, breached-password checks, MFA
options.why: Most common real-world attack.

options.text: Phishing: MFA, preferably WebAuthn passkeys
options.why: A phished password alone is useless.

options.text: Unlimited login attempts are fine because passwords are hashed
options.why: Hashing does not stop online guessing.

options.text: XSS stealing tokens: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies and a strict content security policy
options.why: Keep tokens away from JavaScript.

options.text: Account enumeration: return the same message for unknown user and wrong password
options.why: Do not reveal which emails exist.

steps.title: Log in with Google
steps.prompt: The product adds a 'Log in with Google' button. Which flow?
steps.explain: **OIDC authorization code + PKCE.** Verify the ID token's signature, issuer, audience and expiry; map the Google subject id to your user.

notes: Social login: OIDC authorization code flow with PKCE; link provider subject id to the user

options.text: The implicit flow with tokens in the URL
options.why: Deprecated: tokens leak through browser history and referrers.

options.text: Trust any email the client sends
options.why: No proof of identity.

options.text: OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect **authorization code flow with PKCE**; your server exchanges the code for tokens
options.why: You never see the Google password, and PKCE protects the code.

options.text: Ask the user for their Google password and log in on their behalf
options.why: Exactly what OAuth exists to avoid.

steps.title: Scale and resilience
steps.prompt: Which choices keep authentication available and fast?
steps.hint: What can keep working without the auth service?
steps.explain: The key insight: **token verification needs no auth service**, so an auth outage hurts only new logins, not every API call.

notes: Scale: stateless auth servers, replicated session store and user DB, autoscale hashing, valid tokens survive an auth outage

options.text: Stateless auth servers behind a load balancer across zones
options.why: Add servers for login spikes.

options.text: Separate hashing capacity (autoscale on CPU) from token verification
options.why: They have very different load profiles.

options.text: Graceful degradation: existing valid tokens keep working if the auth service is briefly down
options.why: Verification is local, so only new logins fail.

options.text: User database replicated, sharded by user id if needed, with backups
options.why: Durable and scalable.

options.text: Sessions and rate-limit counters in a replicated Redis
options.why: Shared fast state.

options.text: Everything on one server for simplicity
options.why: A single point of failure for the whole product.

steps.title: Defend your design
steps.prompt: In two or three sentences: what trade-off does the access-plus-refresh token design make?
steps.hint: Fast vs revocable, safe vs convenient.
steps.explain: Always tie the answer back to the **threat you are defending against**.

notes: Trade-offs: stateless speed vs delayed revocation; token lifetime; MFA friction

steps.model: Short-lived **access tokens** give fast, stateless verification at the cost of **delayed revocation** (up to the token lifetime). The **refresh token** brings back control: it is stored server-side so I can revoke it, at the cost of a stateful store on the login and refresh path. Shorter lifetimes are safer but cause more refreshes. MFA improves security but adds friction, so I would apply it based on risk.
points: Lifetime trade-off: security vs more refreshes
